source: Cattell (1943) The measurement of adult intelligence, Psychological Bulletin 40(3)
finding: Cattell first split general ability into fluid (gf) and crystallized (gc). Known here only through the Wikipedia citation; the paper was not read.
numbers: Pages 153-193. No data seen.
limits: Secondhand. Do not quote results from this entry.
agent_relevance: Origin of the idea: Gf is reasoning that does not depend on stored knowledge. Basis for sorting problems by novelty at S0.

source: Wikipedia: Fluid and crystallized intelligence (citing Horn and Cattell 1967)
finding: Gf is solving novel reasoning problems. Gc is applying learned relations. Horn and Cattell 1967 studied age differences: Gf peaks in young adulthood then declines, Gc keeps rising until old age.
numbers: Gf peak about age 27 (described as elusive). Gc stable, declines after about 65. No sample sizes in the article.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, not the 1967 paper (Acta Psychologica 26(2), 107-129). Peak age is disputed.
agent_relevance: Gf versus Gc maps to new problem versus known problem. The S0 gate can use the same split: reason from scratch only when stored knowledge does not apply.

source: Wikipedia: Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory
finding: CHC defines Gf as the broad ability to reason, form concepts and solve problems using unfamiliar information or novel procedures. Gf and Gc are both factors under g. Carroll (1993) reanalysed 461 factor-analytic datasets.
numbers: 461 datasets. The article gives no Gf-to-g loading and no narrow abilities for Gf.
quote: the broad ability to reason, form concepts, and solve problems using unfamiliar information or novel procedures
limits: Thin source for the numbers.
agent_relevance: The definition ('unfamiliar information or novel procedures') is the exact test the S0 gate should apply to a problem.

source: Wikipedia: Fluid and crystallized intelligence, working memory training section
finding: Working memory training was once thought to raise Gf. Later studies did not replicate this. A meta-analysis found short-term, task-specific effects that do not transfer.
numbers: Jaeggi 2008: 70 adults. Chooi and Thompson 2012 and Redick et al. 2012 did not replicate (N not given). Melby-Lervag and Hulme 2012 meta-analysis: no generalisation.
limits: Sample sizes of the failed replications are not in the article.
agent_relevance: Practice on a test format does not build general reasoning. Same lesson as G3: a pass must be on something the answer was not fitted to.

source: Jaeggi, Buschkuehl, Jonides, Perrig (2008) Improving fluid intelligence with training on working memory, PNAS
finding: Dual n-back training for 8 to 19 sessions raised Gf test scores more than no training, with a dose-response pattern. Famous result that later replications did not confirm.
numbers: 70 adults, mean age 25.6, 34 trained. Trained d=0.65, control d=0.25. Group x session F(1,67)=5.27, p<0.05. By days: 17 days F(1,13)=4.65, 19 days F(1,12)=4.53, both p<0.05; 12 days p=0.09. Gf tests: Raven APM (8-day group), BOMAT (others), 10 minutes.
limits: Small groups. Different Gf tests across groups. Passive controls. Controls also gained (d=0.25), so retest effect is large.
agent_relevance: Scores can move through familiarity with the test. Do not treat benchmark gains from prompt tuning as Gf gains.

source: Laurence, Mecca, Serpa, Martin, Macedo (2018) Eye movements and cognitive strategy in a fluid intelligence test, Frontiers in Psychology 9:380
finding: On a matrix test, people who switch less between the matrix and the answer options score higher. Fewer switches means constructive matching (build the answer first). More switches means response elimination.
numbers: N=34 students, 18 items (WMT-2), mean accuracy 58.5% (SD 17.3). Toggling rate vs score r=-0.68, explains 45% of variance. Latency to first toggle r=0.55. Lambda-2 reliability 0.70.
limits: Small sample of students. No working memory measure, so the memory account is untested. An earlier model (Vigneau 2006 MTDI) did not replicate for the full test (R2=0.09).
agent_relevance: Strategy matters as much as ability. For the agent: form the predicted answer from the rule before looking at candidate options; do not choose by elimination.

source: Carpenter, Just, Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures, Psychological Review 97(3):404-431
finding: Computational account of Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices. Per the abstract, two abilities separate high from low scorers: inducing abstract relations and managing many goals in working memory. Full text fetch failed (HTTP 403); only the abstract was seen through a search result.
numbers: No numbers verified this session.
limits: Not opened. Details such as program names are from memory and unverified.
agent_relevance: Difficulty grows with the number of rules and goals held at once, so the schema should keep the goal list in code, not in the model's text.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour
finding: GPT-3 zero-shot matched or beat college students on a text matrix task built on the rule structure of Raven's SPM (Digit Matrices), and on letter-string, verbal and story analogies.
numbers: Digit Matrices: humans N=40 UCLA undergraduates. Generative: GPT-3 beat humans, OR=1.88, p=0.005, CI [1.21,2.91]. Multiple choice OR=6.27, p=2.3e-8. Pattern across problem types correlated with humans r(30)=0.39, p=0.027. Best human got every problem right. SPM comparison sample N=80.
limits: Digit Matrices have no visual parsing. Training-data overlap questioned (a09, a10). Authors do not claim human-like mechanism.
agent_relevance: Frontier text models can do fluid-style rule induction in clean symbols. The weak spot is perception and novelty, not rule induction itself.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Retesting Webb's letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets: humans stay high, GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 drop sharply.
numbers: Human samples: 46 in their data, 57 in Webb. Humans significantly above every GPT model across alphabets. Models mostly pass a comparison check showing they know the new alphabet order, yet still fail the analogies.
limits: Letter-string only. Prompt format from Hodel and West. Webb's reply says code execution closes the gap (a10).
agent_relevance: Fluid reasoning that works only on familiar surface forms is not Gf. The S0 gate should test novelty by changing the surface form, not by asking the model if it feels the problem is new.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Reply to the critiques. On permuted-alphabet problems GPT-4 with code execution reached human level. Digit Matrices already counted as a counterfactual task.
numbers: Human vs GPT-4 alone: significant gap. Human vs GPT-4 + code execution: P=0.496 (no gap). Interval size 2 harder for both. 46% of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule, vs 39% of human errors in Lewis and Mitchell.
limits: Authors defending their own paper. The fix needs code, which humans do not use. Debate is unresolved.
agent_relevance: Code can restore Gf-like performance when the model fails by counting or indexing. Supports routing such steps to code.

source: Moskvichev, Odouard, Mitchell (2023) The ConceptARC Benchmark
finding: ConceptARC has 16 concept groups, 10 tasks each, 3 test inputs per task. Humans far above machine solvers, including GPT-4.
numbers: Overall: humans 91%, first-place Kaggle ARC program 52%, GPT-4 25% (from a later paper, a11). Humans above 90% on 11 of 16 concepts and above 80% on all. GPT-4 under 30% on 15 of 16 concepts. Three guesses allowed.
limits: Text-only grids for GPT-4. Kaggle programs from 2021. Humans from MTurk and Prolific.
agent_relevance: Simple core-knowledge concept tasks still separate model from human. A good sanity set for a novelty gate.

source: Mitchell, Palmarini, Demircan (2023) Comparing humans, GPT-4, and GPT-4V on abstraction and reasoning tasks
finding: With one-shot detailed prompts and text input, GPT-4 still lacks robust abstraction. GPT-4V on image inputs of the simplest tasks was also tested.
numbers: Restates ConceptARC baseline: humans 91%, Kaggle first place 52%, GPT-4 25% (temperature 0.5). Original ARC: Kaggle first place solved 21% of hidden tasks, ensemble 31%.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were checked. GPT-4V numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Better prompts helped only a little at this date. ARC-type tasks need more than a prompt.

source: Gendron, Bao, Witbrock, Dobbie (2023) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners
finding: Across abstract reasoning sets (ARC text, BIG-Bench-F, Evals-S, PVR, RAVEN text), LLMs do poorly in open generation. Fine-tuning on one set gives near-perfect in-distribution scores but does not transfer out of distribution.
numbers: GPT-4 open QA: ARC-T 0.119, BIG-Bench-F 0.514, Evals-S 0.304, PVR 0.177, RAVEN-T text 0.410 / symbolic 0.330. Text-Davinci-3: ARC-T 0.105, RAVEN text 0.343. GPT-3.5-turbo ARC-T 0.033. Small open models near 0. Up to 0.6 with 16 examples on BIG-Bench-F.
limits: 2023 models. Chain-of-thought did not help consistently.
agent_relevance: Training on a task family builds format skill, not Gf. A pass on a familiar family should not lower the novelty flag for a new family.

source: Gendron et al. (2023): fine-tuning transfer
finding: Fine-tuning LLaMA2 on symbolic RAVEN reached 96.5% on the text version of the same task, but accuracy fell sharply when the task itself changed.
numbers: 96.5% on text task after symbolic fine-tune; ARC fine-tune roughly doubles a very low base (base around 0.01 to 0.1).
limits: Doubling a tiny base is small in absolute terms.
agent_relevance: Learning a task family is not Gf.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Reasoning or reciting? Exploring LMs through counterfactual tasks
finding: Eleven task pairs, default vs counterfactual (for example base-10 vs other-base addition). GPT-4 is far better on the default version and drops on counterfactuals while staying above chance.
numbers: GPT-4 0-shot addition accuracy %, 2-digit: base 8 60.2, base 9 38.6, base 10 98.2, base 11 56.5, base 16 74.0. 4-digit: base 10 83.4, base 9 14.6, base 8 24.0, base 11 8.9, base 16 9.1. Drop grows with digit count.
limits: Default is more frequent in training. Some counterfactuals are harder in themselves. Chain-of-thought helps partly.
agent_relevance: Direct measurement of the Gf versus Gc gap in an LLM: same logic, unfamiliar surface, lower accuracy. Usable as a novelty probe at S0.

source: Chollet (2019) On the measure of intelligence
finding: Defines intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency over tasks unknown in advance, given priors and experience. Introduces ARC as a Raven-like fluid intelligence benchmark built on core-knowledge priors.
numbers: ARC: few demonstration grids, predict output grid, three attempts allowed.
quote: the system with higher intelligence is the one that ends up with greater skills
limits: Definition paper. The claim that psychometric-style tests predict broad ability is cited from human literature, not shown for ARC.
agent_relevance: A formal model of Gf for AI. Skill is the output; intelligence is how efficiently priors and experience become skill. The gate should estimate how much prior experience a problem has.

source: LeGris, Vong, Lake, Gureckis (2024) H-ARC: robust estimate of human performance on ARC
finding: Large human baseline on original ARC: humans solve most tasks but not all. Corrects earlier small-sample estimates.
numbers: 1729 participants, 400 training + 400 evaluation tasks. Average 76.2% (range 73.3-77.2) on training, 64.2% (55.9-68.9) on public evaluation. 790 of 800 tasks solved by at least one person within three attempts.
limits: Crowd workers. Lower than earlier estimates (84% in one prior study).
agent_relevance: Human Gf-test performance is not 100%. Compare agent scores to a human distribution, not to a perfect line.

source: ARC Prize 2024 technical report (Chollet, Knoop, Kamradt, Landers)
finding: Test-time training and program search drove the 2024 jump on ARC-AGI-1. Plain static LLMs stayed low.
numbers: Private set top score 33% to 55.5% (MindsAI, not eligible); ARChitects 53.5% (winner). 2020 top score 20%. GPT-3 0% by direct prompting. Semi-private pass@1: o1-preview 18%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14%. No static transduction solution above 11%. Original private tasks: two testers 97% and 98%. 99% of public eval tasks solved by at least one of 10 MTurk workers each.
limits: Gains partly from heavy per-task compute. Some table rows were garbled in text extraction (GPT-4o, Gemini).
agent_relevance: Adapting per task at test time is what lifts novel-task scores. Supports a scaffold that uses task-specific feedback rather than one-shot answers.

source: Chollet et al. (2025) ARC-AGI-2: a new challenge for frontier AI reasoning systems
finding: A harder set built so brute search and memorization fail, with a large first-party human test. Models that do well on ARC-AGI-1 drop to near zero.
numbers: Human testing: 407 participants, 515 sessions, 1,848 task test pairs, 13,405 attempts, 62% solved, median 2.2-2.3 min. Semi-private scores May 2025, ARC-AGI-1 vs ARC-AGI-2: o3 medium 53.0 vs 3.0; o3-mini high 34.5 vs 3.0; o4-mini 41.8 vs 2.4; o1-pro low 23.3 vs 0.9; Claude 3.7 (8K) 21.2 vs 0.9; ARChitects 56.0 vs 2.5. o3 preview 76% and 88% on ARC-AGI-1 at about $200 and $20,000 per task.
limits: Scores under 5% are near noise. Compute-heavy preview numbers were not matched by public versions (o3 medium 53%).
agent_relevance: Fluid tasks with novel rule combinations are still nearly unsolved. Strong reasoning models do not carry over to new compositions.

source: Chollet et al. (2025) ARC-AGI-2, saturation section
finding: A large part of ARC-AGI-1 can be solved by at least one entry or by brute force, so the old set stopped separating systems.
numbers: 2020 competition: 49% of the private set solved by at least one team though best single score was 20%. Humans at the high end solve over 97% of ARC-AGI-1.
limits: Authors' motive for a new version.
agent_relevance: Diverse solvers cover far more than one solver. But samples from one model are correlated (G4).

source: Webb et al. (2023): multi-rule problems
finding: Accuracy fell with the number of unique rules, even with total rules held fixed, for people and GPT-3. Progression rules were harder than others.
numbers: Problem type main effect on generative accuracy OR=0.5, p=2e-16; multiple choice OR=0.56. Progression vs none: humans OR=0.41, p=0.0001; GPT-3 OR=0.07, p=1.9e-5.
limits: Digit Matrices only.
agent_relevance: Count of distinct rules is a usable difficulty signal for the S0 gate and for budgeting attempts.

source: Moskvichev et al. (2023) ConceptARC: per-concept results
finding: Humans score 83% to 97% on every concept. GPT-4 ranges from 3% to 33%.
numbers: Count: humans 0.86, GPT-4 0.03. Center: 0.97 vs 0.20. Inside and Outside: 0.83 vs 0.27. Copy: 0.93 vs 0.07.
limits: One GPT-4 run at temperature 0.5. Counting is hard for text-only models.
agent_relevance: Counting-type sub-skills belong in code.

source: Webb et al. (2023): model variants (supplement)
finding: GPT-3 variants differ widely. code-davinci-002 did well on Digit Matrices and letter strings; others did well on a subset only.
numbers: Variants tested: davinci, code-davinci-002, text-davinci-002, text-davinci-003.
limits: Qualitative statement only; supplement was skimmed.
agent_relevance: Test the exact model used, not a family average.

source: Kambhampati (2024) Can large language models reason and plan?
finding: Position paper arguing LLMs are approximate retrievers and that useful reasoning appears when an LLM is paired with an external verifier in a loop.
numbers: No new experiments in the parts checked.
limits: Opinion, not measured.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema idea of a verifier in the loop (G2, G3).

source: Chuderski and Necka (2012) Contribution of working memory to fluid reasoning: capacity, control or both?
finding: From project notes only: both working-memory capacity and control relate to Gf. Not read.
numbers: Earlier notes list a 62% figure from a snippet; unverified.
limits: Unread.
agent_relevance: Both capacity (how much is held) and control (ignoring distractors) plausibly matter for context design.

source: Kyllonen and Christal (1990) Reasoning ability is (little more than) working memory capacity?!, Intelligence 14
finding: Classic finding that latent working-memory and reasoning factors correlate very highly. Not read this session; number not verified.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Unread. Background only.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping the active context small.
